overview: This file consists of two nearly duplicate “List of Papers” sheets indexing State Department correspondence about interference by Japanese wireless stations with U.S. Army and Navy radio communications in East Asia. The entries trace a proposed informal conference of American and Japanese communications experts in Tokyo, the selection of Captain Fred P. Andrews as the War Department representative, Japanese reluctance to convene such a conference, and debate over whether complaints should be routed through the U.S. Embassy or ordinary diplomatic channels. The indexed correspondence chiefly dates from July 1933 through January 1934, although the sheets themselves are undated.

subfiles.title: First list of papers on wireless telegraph interference in Japan
subfiles.about: An index summarizes correspondence concerning Japanese interference with American military radio stations and proposals for an informal technical conference in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records correspondence from July 29 through January 25 concerning interference by Japanese wireless stations with U.S. Army and Navy communications. It notes War and Navy Department interest in a Tokyo conference, the proposed designation of Captain Fred P. Andrews, Japanese opposition to the conference, and differing views about routing future complaints through the Embassy. Later entries report improved conditions for naval stations but increased interference affecting Army stations and recommend continued use of ordinary diplomatic channels.

subfiles.title: Duplicate list of papers on wireless telegraph interference in Japan
subfiles.about: A second copy of the file index repeats the chronology of official correspondence about Japanese radio interference and the proposed Tokyo conference.
subfiles.summary: This sheet substantially duplicates page 1, again indexing messages about Japanese interference with American Army and Navy radio stations. It records the contemplated October 1933 conference, the Japanese authorities’ view that such a meeting was unnecessary, and the subsequent preference for handling complaints through diplomatic channels. Minor textual differences include identifying the Tokyo despatch as No. 462 rather than No. 463 and presenting parts of the August and September entries with altered table alignment.

interest: The file is useful as a compact docket-level chronology of an early-1930s communications dispute involving American military stations and Japanese transmitters. It shows the practical overlap between technical radio regulation, military communications, and diplomacy, as well as disagreement within the U.S. government over complaint procedures. The two index copies are also valuable for archival criticism because they contain small discrepancies—most notably despatch No. 463 versus No. 462—that may help identify copying, filing, or OCR errors.
